content.thinking:
I'm figuring out how to describe the latency spike without using raw digits, using placeholder labels instead, and starting to trace the chain of events: shoppers experienced slow page loads as p95 latency climbed, while error rates stayed flat.

Working through the causal chain, I find that CPU was pinned at its limit when replica count was low, confirmed by one record, and I want to cite the supporting evidence rows. That low capacity itself was flapping between two core counts every few minutes even though traffic held steady, pointing to the autoscaler scaling down. I trace this to a scale-down stabilization setting reading as zero, though I flag that reading as unverified since it's a static snapshot — I rule out recent deployments or flag changes as causes, note that demand saturation was never directly tested, but the fact that six cores handled the same traffic fine argues against a true capacity ceiling, and the mitigation of raising the floor resolved it. I also note the traffic ramp around a specific timestamp as the likely trigger point, and I'm now trying to land on whether this chain actually reaches a root cause.

I conclude it does reach a cause — a feedback loop explained via the unverified static reading — and move to filling in the duration field, then outlining action items: existing ones, plus new ones around adding a CI test for the scale-down config, alerting on replica-count flapping instead of just raw capacity, and confirming autosync being off is already covered by an existing action item. I also want to flag that the raised floor is a temporary mitigation masking the underlying issue and should be revisited once the real fix merges, and I'm considering whether to add a process item about that.

I'm also being careful to avoid writing bare digits or numeric metric names like "p95" or "5m" in the final text, opting for descriptive phrasing like "tail latency" instead, and double-checking error rate comparisons and other numeric references stay consistent with that rule.

action_items.item: Run the proposed autoscaling config test (scale-down window at least the Kubernetes default, minimum replicas not above maximum) in CI so it runs on every change to the values files. It has not been run yet.
Add an alert on the autoscaler changing replica count back and forth repeatedly within a short period, so flapping pages before or alongside the latency alert.
Once the scale-down window fix is merged and synced, decide whether to keep or lower the raised autoscaler floor, and verify that the replica count stays steady under the same traffic.

causal_chain.step: People using io-shop saw slow responses for {duration}. The tail latency the alert watches rose from {series_before} before onset to {series_while_broken} on average, peaking at {series_at_worst}. The error rate did not rise: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before.

The service was running with too little CPU. In the slow minutes the limit was at the lower of its two values ({C1.1} cores), with CPU pinned at the limit. In the minutes served at the higher value ({C1.2} cores), latency was far lower, even though traffic was the same ({C1.3} rpm).

Capacity would not settle. The CPU limit flipped between {C1.1} and {C1.2} cores every few minutes while traffic held steady. This points to the scaling controller scaling up and then back down, not to a fixed capacity being outgrown.

The controller was set to act on every reading. The scale-down stabilization window in deploy/values-production.yaml is {F1.6}. With the higher replica count, load spreads out and per-replica CPU drops below the {F1.8} target. The controller reads that as falling load and scales back down. The lower count then saturates CPU and latency rises, which triggers the next scale-up. This is a reading of the source only and is unverified, but the confirmed mitigation fits it. Holding the replica floor at the higher count ended the slow period.

The record rules out other triggers. No production changes were read for the day before onset, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. A rise in demand from {C2.1} to {C2.2} rpm from 15:27 was considered as the alternative cause (C2), but that hypothesis was never tried as a mitigation. The same traffic was served well at the higher capacity, which argues against a fixed capacity being outgrown. The record does not show what made the flapping start when it did.

contributing_factors.factor: The scale-down window setting of zero reached production, and no check on the autoscaler settings was seen in the record. A test that would catch it was written only after the incident and has not been run.
Automatic sync of io-shop is off, so nothing merged reaches the service until it is turned back on. The permanent fix cannot reach production by merging alone.
No alert was seen for the replica count or CPU limit flapping. Detection relied on the latency alert, which by its rule waits {rule_waits} before it fires. Flapping would be visible earlier.
The mitigation, a raised autoscaler floor, hides the setting fault. It stays in place, and nothing records when to revisit it.

input.executive_summary: For a short stretch ({duration}) the shop responded much more slowly than usual. Average response times for the slowest requests rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average, and to {series_at_worst} at the worst point. The number of failed requests did not rise: the error rate was {errors_while_broken} against {errors_before} before. People using the shop had slow pages rather than error pages. The service's capacity kept bouncing between a lower and a higher level while traffic was steady. Argus raised the minimum capacity, which kept the service at the higher level, and the metrics returned to normal. A draft fix for the autoscaler setting that most likely caused the bouncing has been proposed and awaits review.

got_lucky: Error rate did not rise, so the harm was slowness and not failed requests.
The flapping was short enough to end quickly once the floor was raised, and traffic was steady rather than climbing further.
went_well: The Investigator placed the onset in the metrics and noticed the capacity flipping between two values. It correctly pointed at the controller.
The mitigation was confirmed by the metrics: the paging rule stopped firing after the floor was raised.
Code-Fix traced the flapping to a specific setting in the repo and proposed a draft fix with a test.
went_wrong: The fix has not been merged, and automatic sync is off, so the root fault remains in the config and the raised floor is the only protection.
The Investigator did not read logs, and the record shows no direct check of the controller's scaling decisions. The mechanism rests on a source reading and the metrics pattern.
The proposed test was not run, since no test runner was available.

input.root_cause: The io-shop autoscaler flapped between a low and a high replica count because its scale-down stabilization window was set to zero in deploy/values-production.yaml. At the higher count, per-replica CPU fell below target and the controller scaled straight back down. At the lower count CPU was pinned at the limit and tail latency rose. This mechanism comes from Code-Fix's reading of the source and the metrics pattern. Nothing ran to verify it, so it is unverified.
input.symptom: Shop pages were slow, with no rise in errors
